experiments.hypothesis: A quadratic trend extrapolates better than a straight line.
A flexible degree-9 polynomial can follow the oscillation and so extrapolates better.
A tiny ridge penalty on the straight line makes its extrapolation more conservative.
Predictions that leave the range of the measurements hurt the score, so clip them to that range.
The readings follow a damped oscillation exp(-g t) (A cos(w t) + B sin(w t)) + C with an unknown decay g and frequency w.
Choosing the polynomial degree and ridge strength by backtesting on the latest part of the training window beats a fixed degree.

requests.summary: I ran 6 lanes in 2 round(s) and asked for 2 independent re-check(s), always for the strongest development gain. These replicated: e001 (A quadratic trend extrapolates better than a straight line.); e005 (The readings follow a damped oscillation exp(-g t) (A cos(w t) + B sin(w t)) + C with an u). These improved on the development data but were not re-checked or did not replicate, so they are not findings: e006. The current best is e005, which replicated. The re-check says only pass or fail, so I report no size for the gain. Caveat: one task, a small pool of measurements, and the development numbers are optimistic because they were used to choose lanes.

lessons.text: e002 ended worse than the incumbent e000 on the dev split (dev delta -530.7, margin 62.37). Train delta +0.1351. The training error improved without a held-out gain: possible overfitting.
e004 was rejected as invalid (protected path violation (workspace)); its result was discarded and only editable files may change.
e003 ended without a gain over the incumbent e000 on the dev split (dev delta +3.139e-08, margin 0.06069). Train delta -2.683e-16.
Models with a functional form matching the physical system extrapolate more safely than extra flexibility.
